parole.significato: place name suffix found in northern Germany
parole.testo: From Middle Low German, from Old Saxon, from the dative plural of a derivative (*būriją?) of Proto-Germanic *būraz (“dwelling”). Cognate with Dutch -buren and perhaps English byre (“barn”). Also related with dated German Bauer (“cage”).
From Middle Low German and Middle Dutch -te, from Proto-Germanic *-iþō, whence also inherited but equally rare German -de.

parole.significato: Placename suffix found chiefly in north-western Germany
parole.testo: With metathesis in the weakened ultima from Middle Low German dorp (“village”), from Old Saxon thorp, from Proto-Germanic *þurpą. While Low German placenames in -dorp were generally standardized with the High German equivalent -dorf, those with the less transparent variant -trop, -trup often remaine

parole.significato: A kind of mediaeval and early-modern tax in some German regions.
parole.testo: From northern Middle High German bede and Middle Low German bēde, from Proto-Germanic *bedō (“plea”). Doublet of Bitte (“plea”). The use for a tax developed in Middle High German.

From Middle Low German binnen (“within”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bi- (“by, at”) + *innan << *in (“in”). The form is also Central German in Middle High German binnen (compare Luxembourgish bannen). It is originally an adverb meaning “within, inside” chiefly in local sense, equivalent to Germ

15th century, from Middle High German bole, or from or akin to Middle Low German bōle (“thick board”, 14th c.), probably from Proto-Germanic *bulaz (“trunk; plank”), and ultimately related to Ball (“ball”). Cognate with Middle Dutch bolle, Old Norse bolr (see there for more), English bole (all “tree
Borrowed from Middle Low German borke, from Proto-Germanic *barkuz. Cognate with Dutch and English bark.
Borrowed from Middle Low German dolle, from Proto-Germanic *þullaz (“thole, rowlock”).

Borrowed from Middle Low German drȫge (“dry”), from Old Saxon *drōgi, from Proto-Germanic *draugiz. Also a Central German form; compare Ripuarian drüch, Luxembourgish dréchen (“dry”). Related to Upper German trocken and, in early modern German, used as a mere dialectal variant of it. In the contempo

Partly from Middle High German esch, ezzisch, from Old High German ezzisc, and partly from Middle Low German esch, *etsch, from Old Saxon etisk, all from Proto-Germanic *atiska- (“grainfield”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *h₂edos- (“sort of cereal, grain”), related to Latin ador (“spelt”), Hit

parole.significato: big dorsal fin as found in large fish and marine mammals
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German finne, vinne, from Old Saxon *finna, from Proto-Germanic *finnō. More at fin.

Borrowed from Middle Low German vlīse, from Proto-Germanic *flīsō (“split chip”), a nasalized dental extension of Proto-Indo-European *(s)pley- (“to split, splice”), whence also Proto-Germanic *splītaną (“to split”). Cognate with Swedish flis (“wood chips”) (DWDS).

15th century (East Prussian), also vluder, from Middle Low German vlundere, from Old Saxon *flunthria, eventually from Proto-Germanic *flunþrijǭ. The High German word must be from Low German given the marine context. However, Low German attestations are equally late and there are some indications th

parole.significato: eyelet; hole for a rope or hook
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German gat, from Proto-Germanic *gatą. Cognate with Dutch gat, English gate. Doublet of Gate.

parole.significato: to desire greedily, to lust for
parole.testo: From Middle High German or Middle Low German gīren (“to open one’s jaws, gape, scream”), from Proto-Germanic *gīran- and ultimately imitative. Cognate with Dutch gieren (“to scream”). Related also with German Geier (“vulture”) and gähnen, English yawn. In standard German, the word has always been as
From Middle Low German glibberich, from a Proto-Germanic base derived from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰelh₃- (“to shine”). Compare Dutch glibberig, English glibbery.
Borrowed from Middle Low German gnitte, from Old Saxon *gnitta, from Proto-Germanic *gnittaz, *gnattaz (“gnat, midge”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰneHdʰn-, *gʰneHd- (“to gnaw, scratch”).

parole.significato: gruit (herbal mixture used in some beers, particularly before the spread of hops)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German grūt, from Old Saxon grūt, from Proto-Germanic *grūtą, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰer- (“to rub, grind”). Cognate with Dutch gruit (whence English gruit), English grout.

15th century, from Middle Low German hakke, from Proto-Germanic *hak(k)-, perhaps related to *hakô. Cognate with Dutch hak. The word also existed in Old High German as hakka (“animal heel”), but this had no attested continuation in Middle High German.

Probably a dialectal variant of Middle Low German ēkel (“disgusting”), from which German Ekel (“loathing, disgust, fastidiousness”). A connection to Proto-Germanic *aikulaz (“fearful”) has been suggested for both words; compare Old English acol (“burdensome, troublesome”), English ache, Galician ext

From Middle Low German helfte, derived from half (“half”). The form entered Early Modern German via Central German. Equivalent to halb (“half”) + -te. The alternation -b- ↔ -ft- has not been levelled, probably because the same alternation occurs also—for different reasons—in native High German words

A Low and Central German word, attested in High German texts from the 15th century. From northern Middle High German *klumpe and Middle Low German klumpe, both from Old Saxon *klumpo, from Proto-Germanic *klumpô (“mass, lump, clump; clasp”), from Proto-Indo-European *glembʰ- (“lump, clamp”). From Middle Low German knap, probably related to Old Norse hneppr (“button”) and hneppa (“pinch”), all from Proto-Germanic *knappô, *knappa-, which is perhaps related to Proto-West Germanic *knappō (“knob, boy”) or Proto-Germanic *knuppaz (“lump, clod”), though the semantic gaps are non-trivial. parole.significato: to crease; to fold; to bend (something that is stable, but not hard, e.g. paper)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German knicken, from Proto-Germanic *knikkōną (“to fold, snap”), which is partly imitative. Cognate with Dutch knikken.

parole.significato: crumb (small broken-off piece, particularly of bread)
parole.testo: Old diminutive of Krume, which is now less common in the simplex form. An originally Central and Low German word that has widely replaced the Upper German Brosame in standard usage. From Middle High German (Central German) krume, reinforced by cognate Middle Low German krume, krōme. From Proto-Germa

From a dialectal variant, from Middle Low German kāk (“stake, rod”), Proto-Germanic *kōpǭ (“the prow of a sleigh”), ultimately related to the root of Kegel. Compare Old Norse kafl, kafli (“an elongated, round piece of wood”), Old Norse kefli (“a roll; scroll”), Middle Low German kavele (“cut wood us

parole.significato: sheet; bed sheet (linen used to cover mattresses or furniture, or sometimes instead of a blanket)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German lāken, from Old Saxon lakan, from Proto-Germanic *lakaną (“sheet, cloth”). The High German cognate Middle High German lachen, from Old High German lahhan, had already been declining in use when the form Laken was introduced during the pre-eminence of the Dutch and Nor

Borrowed from Middle Low German lichten, originally “to make light”, derived from licht (“light; not heavy”). After the Low German development -ft- → -cht- (compare Nichte), the verb was merged with, or at least influenced by, unrelated lüchten (“to lift”), from Proto-Germanic *luftijaną, whence als
From Middle Low German met, from Old Saxon meti (“meal, dish”), from Proto-Germanic *matją, whence also Dutch met. Related with Proto-Germanic *matiz, whence English meat.

From late Middle High German moder (“mold, swamp”), borrowed from Middle Low German modder, modde, mōde (“mud”), from Proto-Germanic *muþraz (“dreg”), from Proto-Indo-European *múHtrom. Doublet of Modder (“mud”), a later borrowing. Cognate with Dutch modder.
From Middle Low German mōr, mūr, from Old Saxon mōr, from Proto-Germanic *mōraz, from Proto-Indo-European. Compare Dutch moer, English moor.

Borrowed from Middle Low German muffen (“to have a moldy smell”), of uncertain ultimate origin, but possibly related to modder (“mud”), from Proto-Germanic *muþraz (“sediment”). However, compare Old High German *muff (“mold”).

Borrowed from Middle Low German nichte, from Old Saxon *nifta, from Proto-Germanic *niftiz. This form replaced High German (obsolete) Niftel in the 17th century. It is based on the Low German shift -ft-→ -cht- (compare Gerücht); hence cognate with Old High German nift, nifta, Dutch nicht, English ni
Late Middle High German, from Middle Low German noppe, from Old Saxon *hnoppo, from Proto-Germanic *hnuppô (“knot in a fabric; tuft or flock of wool”). Compare Dutch nop, Swedish noppa.
Borrowed from Middle Low German packe, from Proto-Germanic *pakkô.

16th century, from Middle Low German pocke, from Proto-Germanic *puhô. Cognate with Dutch pok, English pock. Displaced the variants Poche, Pfoche, which may go back to related Proto-Germanic *puhô, but are perhaps merely inadequate adaptations of the Low German form. The native High German word for
Borrowed from Middle Low German pors, post, from Proto-Germanic *pursaz.

parole.significato: yard (horizontal spar on the mast of a sailing ship)
parole.testo: In the nautical sense (17th c.) from Middle Low German râ, raa, from Proto-Germanic *rahō, *raihô. The spellings in -h, -he may have been influenced by dialectal continuations of cognate Middle High German rahe (“pole, bar”), from Old High German raha; though the insertion of -h- in hiatus or at the

17th century, from Middle Low German *rateren (modern Low German ratern), variant of rettelen, *ratelen, from a frequentative of Proto-Germanic *hratōną. Doublet of German rasseln. See English rattle for more.

parole.significato: ray (marine fish with a flat body, large wing-like fins, and a whip-like tail)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German roche, ruche, possibly a derivative of Proto-Germanic *rūhwaz (“rough”), but often thought to be from a substrate (compare also Latin raia). Cognate with Dutch rog, Old English reohhe, ruhha, and, via Old French, English roach (“a fish”).

From northern Middle High German roten, roden and Middle Low German rōden, from Proto-Germanic *rudōną, which is related to *raupijaną (“to rip out, pluck”), *reufaną (“to tear”). Cognate with Dutch rooien. Also akin to English rid, Danish rydde. The variant rotten (still in ausrotten) shows a more

parole.significato: stale (of food and drink: having lost its taste through age, oxidation, etc.)
parole.testo: From (late and northern) Middle High German schal (“tasteless, turbid”), borrowed from Middle Low German schal, from Proto-Germanic *skal-, derived from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelh₁- (“to dry out”). Compare Swedish skäll (“thin, weak, bleak”), Old English sċeald (“shallow, flat”), whence modern Eng
From northern Middle High German schihten, from Middle Low German schichten, from Old Saxon *skiftian, from Proto-Germanic *skiftijaną. Cognate with Dutch schiften, English shift.

A Central and Low German word, from northern Middle High German *schüppe (attested 15th c.) and Middle Low German schüppe, from Proto-Germanic *skupjō. Cognate with Luxembourgish Schëpp (“shovel”), Dutch schop (“shovel, spade”).

From Middle Low German slap (“flaccid”), from Proto-Germanic *slap-, perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)leh₂b- (“to be weak, limp, languid”), and from the same family of words as German *slēpaną (“to sleep”); see also Latin labō (“fluctuate, waver”). parole.significato: clever in a way that enables one to achieve one's goals; slightly sly or cunning (but not usually implying any evil int…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German slû, whence probably also Dutch sluw. Further origin uncertain. Probably from a Proto-Germanic *slūhaz (“sneaking, creeping”), which seems to trace back to a Proto-Indo-European *(s)lewǵ- (“to crawl, slide”) (albeit without any known extra-Germanic cognates), if the o

parole.significato: need, privation, especially hunger or thirst
parole.testo: From rare, northern Middle High German smaht, later reinforced by Middle Low German smacht. Derived from the adjective Proto-Germanic *smēhaz (“little, small”). Related to Schmach.

parole.significato: to suffer hardship, especially severe hunger or thirst
parole.testo: First attested in the 17th century, from Schmacht + -en, after Middle Low German smachten. The noun and the prefixed verb verschmachten are also attested in northern Middle High German (smaht, versmahten). Ultimately derived from the adjective Proto-Germanic *smēhaz (“small, little”). Related with A

Borrowed from Middle Low German smuk (“supple, bendsome, pleasing, beautiful, petite, cute”) (compare Middle Low German smuk (“ornament, jewellery”)), from Old Saxon *smuk, *smukk, from Proto-Germanic *smukkaz (“flexible, bendsome, easy”).

From Schupp (“push”) + -s (“intensive nominal ending”). Schupp (15th c.) is deverbal from northern Middle High German and Middle Low German schuppen, from Proto-Germanic *skuppōną, intensive form of *skeubaną, whence German schieben and English shove. See schubsen for more.

parole.significato: to shove (to give a rough push, especially to another person)
parole.testo: 19th c., denominal from Schubs, Schupps (“push”), from Schupp (“push”) + -s (“intensive nominal ending”). Schupp (15th c.), in turn, is deverbal from northern Middle High German and Middle Low German schuppen, from Proto-Germanic *skuppōną, intensive form of *skeubaną, whence German schieben and Eng
Deverbal from northern Middle High German and Middle Low German schuppen, from Proto-Germanic *skuppōną, intensive form of *skeubaną.

parole.significato: to shove, to push, to hustle
parole.testo: From northern Middle High German and Middle Low German schuppen, from Proto-Germanic *skuppōną, intensive form of *skeubaną, whence German schieben and English shove. See schubsen for more.

parole.significato: swath, windrow (row of cut grain or hay; both cut out herbage and the left empty space)
parole.testo: From northern Middle High German swade and Middle Low German swade, both from Proto-Germanic *swaþō, possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swey- (“to bend, turn, swing”). See English swath for more.

The word was originally restricted to Low and Central German: from Middle High German spade, spate and Middle Low German spade, both from Old Saxon spado (possibly also Old High German *spato), from Proto-Germanic *spadô. Due to its northern origin the form has undergone open-syllable lengthening be

parole.significato: collective word for apparitions or actions of ghosts, haunting, supernatural (usually frightening) occurrences
parole.testo: 17th century, from Middle Low German spōk, from Old Saxon *spōk, from Proto-Germanic *spōk. Cognate with Dutch spook, whence English spook.
Borrowed from Middle Low German steven (“stick, support”), ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *stamniz (“tree stalk”).

From Middle Low German stîge (also stēge), from Old Saxon stīga (“pigsty”). Possibly a byform of Proto-Germanic *stiją, whence English sty, but definitely related with it (compare *stīganą (“to climb”)), or otherwise possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *steyh₂- (“to stiffen”), similar to *s

parole.significato: sound, strait (especially near islands of the Baltic Sea)
parole.testo: From Middle High German sunt (ca. 1300), borrowed from Middle Low German sunt, from Proto-Germanic *sundą.
Borrowed from Middle Low German touw, from Old Saxon tou, from Proto-Germanic *tawwą. Related to English tow.

parole.significato: to tap, to strike lightly (often repeatedly)
parole.testo: From Middle Low German tippen (“to touch lightly”), from Middle Low German tip (“tip, fingertip”), cognate with English tip, from Proto-Germanic *tuppijô, *tuppijǭ (“tip”), diminutive of *tuppaz (“top”). Merged with Central and Low German tippen, dippen, düppen (“to dip, to dab, to tap”), from Proto

parole.significato: midnight mass or early morning mass (at Christmas and Easter)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German uchte, from Old Saxon ūhta, from Proto-Germanic *unhtwǭ. Related to Dutch ochtend (“morning”).

From Middle High German uover, ūver, ūber, possibly from northern Old High German *uofar, but usually considered a borrowing from Middle Low German ōver, ȫver, from Old Saxon *ōvar, *ōvir, from Proto-Germanic *ōferaz. Cognate with Dutch oever, Low German Över, English over (“shore, riverbank”). The

parole.significato: to immerse, submerge, duck; (especially) to duck someone else’s head under water
parole.testo: From unter- + Low German döppen, düppen. The latter is from Middle Low German düppen, from Proto-Germanic *dupjaną, whence also German tupfen, (partially) tippen, and (via English) dippen.

parole.significato: to wobble, wiggle, jiggle; said of jelly/jello, human body fat, and the like
parole.testo: From Middle High German wabelen, merged with related Middle Low German *wabbelen. To the former compare Old Norse vafla, to the latter dialectal Dutch wobbelen, English wabble, wobble. All of these are iteratives of Proto-Germanic *wabōną, related to *webaną (“to weave”), whence Middle High German w

parole.significato: a naturally formed open spot in the ice cover of a body of water
parole.testo: 17th century, from Middle Low German wāke, from Proto-Germanic *wakwō.

parole.significato: intertidal zone, foreshore, especially the vast mudflats at the North Sea coast
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German wat, from Proto-Germanic *wadą.

parole.significato: a farmer whose land has been independent property since medieval times (therefore generally richer and formerly entitle…
parole.testo: From Middle Low German teller, tēler, derived from tēlen (“to cultivate”), from Proto-Germanic *tilōną (whence also Dutch telen). From Middle High German twenge and Middle Low German dwenge (“constraint, clamp; lace”), from Proto-Germanic *þwanguz, *þwangiz, cognate with English thong, German Zwang.
